summary: Defines an ISAKMP Domain of Interpretation for group key management. The GDOI manages group security associations used to protect group communications, such as IPsec traffic. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 6407.

eli5.summary: When a group wants to share secret messages, everyone needs the same key. This memo defines how a group gets and updates that key safely.

questions: how does group key management work
what is forward access control in multicast
how does gdoi protect multicast traffic
subtitle: Manage encryption keys for secure group communications and multicast applications.

tldr.problem: Secure multicast and group communications require all members to share encryption keys, but managing and distributing these keys securely among a dynamic group is complex. Existing protocols like IKE are designed for point-to-point communication, not for group scenarios.
tldr.mechanism: GDOI defines a Domain of Interpretation (DOI) for ISAKMP that enables two main exchanges: GROUPKEY-PULL, where a group member requests keys from a Group Controller/Key Server (GCKS), and GROUPKEY-PUSH, where the GCKS securely distributes new or updated keys to all group members. GDOI manages both Key Encrypting Keys (KEKs) for encrypting future key updates and Traffic Encrypting Keys (TEKs) for the actual data encryption.
tldr.outcome: Group applications can establish secure multicast sessions and manage dynamic membership changes while maintaining access control. Removed members cannot decrypt new group keys, and new members cannot decrypt old group data. GDOI was superseded by RFC 6407, which modernizes the specification with more recent security practices.

facts.value: KEK (Key Encrypting Key) and TEK (Traffic Encrypting Key)

today: RFC 3547 was superseded by RFC 6407 (GDOI Version 2), which updates the specification with support for IKEv2 as an alternative Phase 1 mechanism and incorporates improvements based on implementation experience. GDOI concepts remain foundational for secure multicast and group communications, though new implementations should follow RFC 6407.

sections.title: Secure Group Communications
sections.content: Secure multicast is essential for many applications: video broadcast, multicast file transfer, and collaborative applications all require efficient distribution of data to multiple recipients while ensuring confidentiality and integrity. In a business environment, many such applications use IPsec to protect their traffic. However, the challenge is managing the encryption keys for the group. Unlike point-to-point communication where two parties negotiate keys, group communication requires a key distribution mechanism that can efficiently handle dynamic group membership: members joining and leaving without compromising the security of either new or previous communications. GDOI solves this by defining how group members and a central group controller work together to establish and maintain security associations for the entire group.
sections.eli5: A group video broadcast needs a key so only members can watch. When someone leaves, the group needs a new key so they cannot watch future broadcasts. GDOI is the protocol that handles all of this automatically.

sections.title: GDOI Concepts and Architecture
sections.content: GDOI defines the interaction between group members (entities that want to participate in group communication) and a Group Controller/Key Server (GCKS) (the entity that manages group keys and policy). The GCKS maintains a database of group information and is responsible for creating, distributing, and updating security associations. GDOI distinguishes between two types of keys: Key Encrypting Keys (KEKs), which protect the distribution of other keys, and Traffic Encrypting Keys (TEKs), which are used by IPsec or other data security protocols to encrypt actual group traffic. The GDOI protocol runs in two phases. Phase 1 establishes an authenticated, encrypted session between the member and the GCKS using ISAKMP. Phase 2 uses two new message types: GROUPKEY-PULL, where a member actively requests group keys, and GROUPKEY-PUSH, where the GCKS proactively sends new keys to all members. This architecture supports both pull-based initialization and push-based key updates.
sections.eli5: A GCKS is like a trusted key master. Members ask it for keys (pull), and the GCKS also sends out new keys when the group changes (push). Keys for encrypting keys are separate from keys for encrypting data, which is more flexible.

sections.title: GROUPKEY-PULL and GROUPKEY-PUSH
sections.content: When a group member wants to join a group, it initiates a GROUPKEY-PULL exchange with the GCKS. This is a four-message exchange protected by the Phase 1 security association. The member sends a first message with its group identity and a nonce (a random value to prevent replay attacks). The GCKS responds with the group's security policy, including the algorithms and key lengths for the KEK and any TEKs, along with another nonce. The member then sends a third message that may include a certificate proving its authorization to join the group, along with a Proof of Possession (POP) payload that demonstrates the member holds the secret key associated with that certificate. Finally, the GCKS sends a fourth message containing the actual key material in the Key Download (KD) payload. Once a member has keys, the GCKS uses GROUPKEY-PUSH messages for ongoing key management. These are sent encrypted with the current KEK so only current members can decrypt them. When group membership changes, new KEKs are distributed via GROUPKEY-PUSH, and subsequent TEKs are sent with the new KEK, ensuring removed members cannot access future traffic.
sections.eli5: A member asking for keys starts with a handshake: both sides prove they are real and alive, then the GCKS sends back the keys. Later, the GCKS sends push messages to update keys. When someone leaves, they cannot decrypt the new keys anymore.

sections.title: Payloads and Message Structure
sections.content: GDOI uses ISAKMP as its foundation and defines several new payload types. The SA (Security Association) payload describes the cryptographic policies for the group, followed by SA KEK (SAK) payloads for re-key SA policy and/or SA TEK (SAT) payloads for data-security SA policy. The Identification (ID) payload carries the group identity, which may be a four-octet group ID or a longer identifier. The Key Download (KD) payload contains the actual key material corresponding to the policies described in the SA payloads. The Sequence Number (SEQ) payload tracks the order of GROUPKEY-PUSH messages, ensuring members do not install keys out of order. The Proof of Possession (POP) payload validates that a member or the GCKS possesses the secret key associated with a certificate, protecting against impersonation. The Nonce (N) payload provides replay protection. All messages are protected by ISAKMP with encryption occurring after the message header for GROUPKEY-PULL and GROUPKEY-PUSH messages.
sections.eli5: GDOI messages are built from standard blocks (payloads). Each payload carries specific information: who is talking, what policies apply, what the actual keys are, and proof that everything is legitimate.

sections.title: Access Control and Key Hierarchy
sections.content: A key feature of GDOI is its support for access control based on group membership. Forward access control ensures that when a member is removed from the group, it cannot decrypt traffic encrypted with keys created after its removal. Backward access control prevents a new member from decrypting traffic that was encrypted before it joined the group. GDOI achieves this through careful key management. When group membership changes, the GCKS creates a new KEK and distributes it via GROUPKEY-PUSH encrypted with the old KEK. Only current members have the old KEK and can decrypt the new KEK. The removed member cannot decrypt the new one and thus cannot access subsequent traffic. New members only receive keys from the moment they join, so they cannot access historical traffic. For large groups or frequent membership changes, the Logical Key Hierarchy (LKH) algorithm reduces the number of keys that must be distributed. Instead of giving each member an individual key, LKH uses a tree structure where group members hold only a path of keys through the tree, reducing the number of keys distributed during membership changes from O(N) to O(log N).
sections.eli5: Removed members cannot see new movies because they do not get the new key. New members cannot see old movies because they never got those old keys. This is like physically handing over a door key only to current trusted members.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limitations
sections.content: GDOI provides strong security properties through its reliance on ISAKMP Phase 1. The Phase 1 SA establishes peer authentication, message confidentiality, and message integrity protection. Nonces in both GROUPKEY-PULL and GROUPKEY-PUSH protect against replay attacks. The SIG payload in GROUPKEY-PUSH messages provides authentication of key updates, preventing attackers from injecting false keys into the group. GDOI supports Perfect Forward Secrecy through optional Diffie-Hellman exchanges. However, GDOI requires a trusted GCKS: if the GCKS is compromised or acts maliciously, the security of all group keys is compromised. The protocol also assumes secure Phase 1 authentication; the security of GDOI is no better than the security of the underlying ISAKMP Phase 1 mechanism. Additionally, while GDOI can establish security associations for multicast traffic, it does not inherently prevent all denial-of-service attacks; a malicious group member with a valid KEK could still send unauthorized messages to the group. RFC 3547 was superseded by RFC 6407 (GDOI Version 2), which updated the specification to use more modern security practices and added support for IKEv2 as an alternative Phase 1 mechanism.
sections.eli5: GDOI is as secure as its Phase 1 setup. If the GCKS is trustworthy and Phase 1 is secure, the keys are safe. But if someone gets the old key after being removed, they can read old messages. GDOI was updated to RFC 6407 with modern improvements.
